title: 报告：Steam前八个月收入达150亿美元，“中端市场”扩大是真正增长极
text:
【GameLook专稿，禁止转载！】
GameLook报道/Steam 收入又创下了新纪录。海外数据平台Alineaanalytics近日公布的数据显示，2026年迄今为止，Steam平台的游戏收入已经达到150亿美元，同比增长15%。仅仅前8个月，收入就已经超过了2023全年，且预计全年收入首次突破200亿美元。
以下是Gamelook编译的完整内容：
Steam 是一头巨兽。Valve 在 PC 市场近乎垄断的地位，让其今年迄今的总收入已达 150 亿美元——较 2025 年同期增长约 15%。
今年前八个月的收入已经超过了 2023 年全年。今年的总收入几乎肯定会首次大幅突破 200 亿美元。
不过不太好的消息是，Steam 今年已有 1.9 万款新游戏发售，已经逼近 2025 年全年的数量，并超过了 2024 年……而席卷而来的生成式 AI 垃圾内容大潮也迫在眉睫。
不过这就是另一个故事了。
截至目前，2026 年 Steam 营收最高的新游戏有哪些？
无论从哪个角度看，2026 年对 Steam 上的新游戏来说都是一个极其精彩的一年，还有更多重磅炸弹即将到来。您可以看看我们对 2026 年 Steam 营收最高新游戏的预估排名：
不过整体来看，这六款游戏今年的 Steam 总收入加起来接近 10 亿美元，占 2026 年 Steam 总营收的约 6.6%。
2026 年新游戏营收前 100 名的总收入约为 24 亿美元，占今年 Steam 总营收的约 15.9%。在新游戏前 100 名中，63% 实际上属于全新 IP，但营收的 52.5%（约 12.5 亿美元）来自已有 IP。
不过值得注意的是，Crimson Desert 凭借 2.03 亿美元的收入，占了前 100 名全新 IP 总收入的约 18%。如果把 Crimson Desert 剔除，剩下 62 款全新 IP 游戏只占约 39%。可见这份榜单里有很多中端市场的全新 IP 游戏。
再来说到中端市场……
Steam 的”中端市场”主要是一群披着新衣的旧日爆款
上个月，Joost van Dreunen（笔者个人心目中的英雄之一，也是 Alinea 的朋友）一如既往地发表了一篇精彩文章——《Steam 中端市场的复仇》。如果还没看过，强烈推荐一读。这篇文章对今年 PC 经济格局的变化观察得相当敏锐。
简单来说，他的论点是：全球最大 PC 游戏商店的增长，已经不再是流向头部爆款，而是开始流向中端。
Joost 说得对，老游戏在发售目录中的占比确实越来越大。但关于文章中的一部分，我想补充一下。他把整个排名 101 到 1000 名区间的 Steam 游戏都归入了中端市场。
尽管那榜单里确实有很多中端游戏，但也有很多是多年前就已发行、如今在发售多年后逐渐下滑的昔日巨作。这是我读到那篇精彩文章时脑海中浮现的第一反应，一些评论者也指出了这一点。
我们结合 Alinea 对 2026 年 Steam 营收前 1000 名游戏的预估，以及每款游戏的首次发行日期和迄今为止的终生总收入，将目光聚焦在排名 101 到 1000 名的 900 款游戏上。有几点颇为突出：
相对而言，它们确实属于中端市场：仅看 2026 年的营收，把这些游戏归为中端市场是合理的。这批游戏中位数营收约 400 万美元——从第 101 名的 1990 万美元到榜尾的 190 万美元。我也觉得相当”中端”。
但它们大部分是老游戏：这 900 款中，83% 在 2026 年之前就已发行，三分之二甚至已经是两年以上的老游戏，只有 17% 是 2026 年发售的新作。这里有很多老库存游戏的成分。自发行以来终生总收入超过 5000 万美元的游戏，占这批游戏 2026 年营收的 51%。所以这主要是老库存游戏的贡献，而不是一个冉冉升起的新中端。
老牌爆款比比皆是： 约三分之一的游戏终生总收入超过 5000 万美元，22.3% 超过 7500 万美元，140 款超过 1 亿美元，5.2% 超过 2 亿美元。而且这还只是 Steam 的数据。这些游戏中，有不少在其他平台同样创造了可观的收入。
榜单中也有不少中端游戏：不过榜单中也有相当比例的我心目中的中端市场游戏，包括 Mortal Shell II（重磅炸弹）、Hell Let Loose: Vietnam 和 The Seven Deadly Sins: Origin。
但当你看看榜单上其他游戏时，那些爆款的数量不容忽视：
这些游戏也绝非精挑细选出来的。Skyrim、Battlefield 2042、The Elder Scrolls Online、DOOM Eternal、Assassin’s Creed Origins、Devil May Cry 5、Total War: Warhammer II、Rise of the Tomb Raider、Metro Exodus 以及许多其他标志性作品也都赫然在列。
那么这一切说明了什么？
“前 10 名收窄、中端市场扩大”这一论点，只有在中端由新的中等规模游戏构成时才成立。但我们的预估显示，事实并非如此。一款游戏目前在 Steam 上的排名，并不能真正说明它是什么样的游戏。
一款游戏今年在 Steam 上营收 400 万美元，如今看起来像中端市场，但如果是几年前基于 1 亿美元预算打造、生涯总收入超 2 亿美元的大作，跟一支预算仅 500 万美元的 AA 小团队作品，根本就不是一个物种。它们只不过碰巧在 2026 年的榜单上挨在一起罢了。
尽管（尤其在 Steam 上）有不少中等规模和独立游戏的重磅作品，但市场在很大程度上仍然是由爆款驱动的。只不过这些爆款中有很多是多年前的作品，如今以折扣价格出售（老实说，这是 Steam 最具性价比的卖点之一）。
这些并不是要否定 Joost 的观点——只是为这篇精彩文章补充一些更丰富的细节（行业里需要更多这样的文章）。

title: Revenge of Steam's mid-market
author: Joost van Dreunen
text:
Revenge of Steam's mid-market
Gamers are spending more on games than ever. They're just not new
ones.
· Aug 18, 2026
Original article: https://superjoost.substack.com/p/revenge-of-steams-mid-market
The
SuperJoost Playlist is a weekly take on gaming, tech, and entertainment by business professor and author 
Joost van Dreunen.
While putting together my itinerary for Cologne, I came across its upcoming kick-off event, Gamescom
Opening Night Live 2026. It reminded me of something Geoff Keighley said during the Summer Game Fest
live stream from a few months ago.
During his opening monologue in June, he pointed out the sheer volume of new games being published each
year. Quoting GameDiscoverCo’s data, he told the audience that 9,265 new games had been released on
Steam in the first five months of 2026, up from 7,800 the year before.
Keighley preempted the obvious objection: “A cynic might look at those numbers and think, ‘How can
anyone possibly break through?’”
He then answered with fourteen success stories: new releases that had already sold over a million copies,
including Mewgenics, Slay the Spire II (one of my favorites), Vampire Crawlers, and Windrose.
1
Here’s a different answer: those fourteen games amount to just 0.15 percent of releases, and it’s not where the
bulk of consumer spending went. Yes, in the first half of 2026, overall Steam sales grew by $1.41 billion.
New releases accounted for none of the growth.
TL;DR
Steam revenue grew $1.41 billion (+14.5 percent) from H1 2025 to H1 2026, but back-catalog
sales added $1.80 billion while new releases shrank by $0.39 billion. The catalog drove more
than 100 percent of the growth. Overall, new launches were a net negative.
Steam’s top 10 titles peaked in 2023 at $4.3 billion and have declined since. Mid-market titles
(ranked 101 to 1,000) quadrupled from $1.1 billion in 2019 to $4.5 billion in 2025. The
blockbuster tier is stalling while everything between the top 10 and the tail is growing.
Existing titles’ share of total Steam revenue rose from 71 percent to 78 percent in a single
year. New releases fell from $2.79 billion to $2.40 billion (-14 percent).
People are buying old games, but not playing them. On a same-game panel of 16,565 pre-2024
titles, spending rose 26 percent while average daily players per game fell 10 percent. Rather
than a catalog renaissance, however, this is backlog inflation.
• 
• 
• 
• 
2
• 
• 
Every new release now competes against everything ever made, at a discount. This raises the
risk profile of blockbusters without lowering their ceiling: GTA VI is fine, but the mid-tier
AAA releases are not.
This is the distribution-innovation phase of the Play Pendulum: consumers hunt for cheaper
alternatives (low-tech, low-brow, low-cost), and audience-owning creatives thrive while high
cost, long-timeline publishers squeeze.
Blockbuster consensus
Since the pandemic, publishers have become more risk-averse. Instead of releasing risky, innovative titles,
they prefer to rely on established franchises. Like Hollywood, the games industry prefers sequels that signal
quality and reduce demand uncertainty.
At a time when the entire industry is holding its breath for the release of Grand Theft Auto VI, wintering
through a soft period by betting on blockbusters seems the obvious choice. Investors love it. Audiences love
it. What’s not to like?
Plenty of theory backs this up. Anita Elberse, a Harvard Business School professor, described in her 2013
book, Blockbusters: Hit-making, Risk-taking, and the Big Business of Entertainment, how concentrating
budgets on a few likely winners beats carefully managing a broad portfolio, which merely produces marginal
results. Blockbusters, she found, were not a gamble but a hedge.
Elberse was arguing against Chris Anderson’s 2006 long-tail thesis. As entertainment became increasingly
digitized, he theorized that infinite shelf space would let niche titles collectively outsell the hits. Even small
productions could assemble financially sustainable audiences worldwide thanks to digital distribution. For a
decade, the evidence has sided with Elberse. Music and film were digitized, and demand was concentrated
into fewer, bigger hits, exactly as she predicted.
Then there’s Steam.
According to GYLD, an Australian games agency (disclosure: I’m an advisor and investor), the world’s
largest PC gaming storefront has stopped following Elberse’s script. In the first half of 2026, Steam generated
$11.1 billion in revenue, up $1.41 billion from the previous year. Yet none of that growth came from new
releases. Back-catalog sales added $1.80 billion while new releases shrank by $0.39 billion, falling from
$2.79 billion to $2.40 billion. Existing games drove more than 100 percent of the platform’s growth. Overall,
new launches were a net negative.
3
Can't catalog sales just be blockbuster sales?
Fair question. New-versus-old and hit-versus-niche are different axes. If the $8.7 billion catalog were
dominated by GTA V, Baldur’s Gate 3, and a handful of evergreen live-service giants, Elberse would be
winning after all. Old blockbusters eating new blockbusters is still a blockbuster economy, just one with its
back turned to the release calendar.
That’s not what GYLD’s numbers show.
4
Steam’s top 10 titles earned $4.0 billion in 2025, down from a peak of $4.3 billion in 2023, and falling for
two consecutive years. As a share of the platform, the blockbuster tier has slid from roughly 41 percent in
2019 to 28 percent in 2025. Meanwhile, the mid-market, titles ranked 101 to 1,000, quadrupled from $1.1
billion to $4.5 billion over the same period. Add the hits tier (ranked 11 to 100), and the middle of the market
earned $9.0 billion in 2025, more than double the top 10 combined.
You’ll notice the long tail here: everything ranked 1,001 and below grew sevenfold since 2019 to $1.5 billion.
Impressive, yes, but still just 10 percent of the platform.
Here’s where that leaves us. Both Anderson and Elberse took extreme positions on what would drive growth
in a digital marketplace. In 2026, on the largest PC storefront in the world, the answer sits between their
extremes: titles ranked 11 to 1,000 earned $9.0 billion in 2025, more than double the top 10, and grew while
the blockbuster tier shrank.
Buying the backlog, yes, but not playing it
There’s a second twist here, which feels both intuitively correct and odd. People are buying all these old
games. They are not, it turns out, playing them. Think of it as backlog inflation, rather than a catalog
renaissance.
That seems totally on brand for Steam players. A 2014 analysis by Kyle Orland (who I forgot to add to my 
hero list of game journalists. Sorry, Kyle!) showed that buying and playing were two different things on
Steam. 
5
On a same-game panel of 16,565 pre-2024 titles measured across both 181-day halves, catalog spending rose
26 percent while average daily players per game fell 10 percent. Twenty years into the argument between
Anderson and Elberse's extremes, it turns out people buy as Anderson predicted and play as Elberse did.
Thanks to SuperJoost Playlist’s paying subscribers, this week’s BIG READ is free for everyone. If
you’d like more of the industry’s numbers explained and want these pieces to keep coming, consider
joining them.
What does this mean for blockbuster releases?
I’ve previously written about the changing stance among players toward games: low-tech, low-brow, and
low-cost. Yes, we have GTA VI, and it’ll be amazing. But game costs keep creeping up for consumers, in both
hardware and software. Where console makers can improve their margins by eliminating physical carriers and
pocketing refunds after suing over the tariffs imposed in early 2025, consumer prices only go up. No surprise,
then, that demand for cheaper alternatives is growing.
It raises the stakes for big launches. Every new release competes against everything ever made, most of it at a
steep discount, and much of it destined for a backlog that will never be played.
None of this lowers the ceiling for marquee titles like Marvel’s Wolverine or GTA VI. They will do enormous
numbers. What does change is the floor, and the odds for everyone below the very top. The mid-tier AAA
release at $70 now competes with last year’s Game of the Year at $25 and a decade of classics at $10. If,
following Elberse’s logic, a blockbuster strategy was supposed to be the hedge, it is losing its efficacy.
All this fits the pattern I’ve described as the Play Pendulum. The industry swings between phases of content
innovation and distribution innovation. In the distribution phase we’re in, consumers hunt for cheaper
alternatives, and creatives who own an audience thrive, while large publishers struggle with high
development costs and ever-longer timelines.
Prediction
Assuming this two-year trend continues, Steam’s top 10 titles will account for less than 25 percent of
platform revenue by EOY 2027.
The blockbuster tier’s share has declined from roughly 41 percent in 2019 to 28 percent in 2025, and its
absolute revenue has declined for two straight years since the freak 2023 cohort of Baldur’s Gate 3, Hogwarts
Legacy, and Starfield. 
6
For the prediction to miss, the top of the market needs a 2023-scale year, twice, in the window when GTA VI
is pulling full-price spending toward console. Meanwhile, everything below the top 10 keeps compounding:
every title that succeeds joins the catalog, where it sells at a discount forever, deepening the shelf the next
blockbuster competes against.
That brings me back to Geoff. 
He’s right that fourteen games clearing a million copies is worth celebrating, and right that players show up
for bold creative swings. What he didn’t mention, standing in front of the industry’s biggest annual showcase
of what’s next, is that the audience has been redirecting its money toward what already exists. Major events
like Summer Game Fest, Opening Night Live, and The Game Awards are built around selling The New.
Audiences, meanwhile, are buying the old.
Keighley’s question shouldn’t have been “How can anyone possibly break through?” A better one is “Who
are new games actually competing against?” The short answer here is a shelf they’ll have to share with
everything ever made, at prices they can't feasibly match, in backlogs that never shrink.
Let's find out whether anyone on stage in Cologne will be asking it. 
See you there

title: Does your Steam demo CCU ‘predict’ your game’s success?
text:
Discover more from The GameDiscoverCo newsletter
Analysis, data and insight about how people find & buy video games in the 2020s.

Does your Steam demo CCU ‘predict’ your game’s success?
We’ve got data. Unsurprisingly. Also: lots of news & new GameDiscoverCo Show.
Simon Carless
Sep 09, 2026
[The GameDiscoverCo game discovery newsletter is written by ‘how people find your game’ expert & company founder Simon Carless, and is a regular look at how people discover and buy video games in the 2020s.]
We’re right back at it, and we’re wondering how y’all doing out there. Reasonable? OK? Hunky dory? We’re… how do you say… rather excited to get on with our job, which is providing you much info on why video games are popular. So we’ll do that!
Before we start, the runaway ‘silly story’ intro slot winner this week: “ Elden Ring Director Hidetaka Miyazaki Says He’s ‘Honestly Not Sure’ Where the Rumor About Him Having a Foot Fetish Came From .” Good job, IGN (and The Guardian for doing The Duskbloods interview .) So no, plz don’t call Miyazaki ‘ Tarantino-esque’ …
[ NEED THE BEST DATA? You can get a free demo of our GameDiscoverCo Pro company-wide ‘Steam deep dive’ & console data, inc. MCP server, by reaching out today - >110 orgs have it. Or, signing up to GDCo Plus gets extra newsletter and Discord access, plus more .]
Game discovery news: summon the Wardogs…
Let’s take a look at some of the more notable game platform & discovery news since late last week, as follows:
Here's GDCo Pro estimates of 'trending' unreleased Steam games by 'new wishlists in the last 7 days' , Sept 1st-7th - and 'friendslop in the air' standout Dear Passengers (#1) and tactical shooter Wardogs (#3) shouldn’t be a surprise (We’ve talked less about F2P ARPG creature collector Aniimo (#2), which has good momentum.)
At #4, The Missing Tail , from Estoty (creators of VR/mobile hit I Am Cat ) does the 'two player co-op only' thing with cozy cat shenanigans, getting ~100k wishlists in no time. And PlayStation's State Of Play helped Final Fantasy VII Revelation (#5) and FF: Resonance (#9), as well as killer shark sequel Maneater 2 (#8) trend.
According to data provided to The Game Business , “The GTA 6 Netflix reveal has caused a spike in sales of PlayStation and Xbox hardware. According to Nielsen IQ, UK PS5 sales jumped 33% [in the week following the reveal], while Xbox Series S and X sales leapt 34%.” The public, they love grand theft-ing in their autos…
Over on Facebook (!) former Epic wunderkind Cliff Bleszinski has views on the ‘Crash 2.0 for games ’ rhetoric: “So is the end near? Hardly. ‘Life finds a way”’ - keep looking towards the AA/’slop’ area to find the fun, and at a reasonable price, which allows you to sample a bunch of quirky, innovative titles with friends. Let AAA faceplant for a while, I say.”
Spotting smaller Steam games getting more front page referrer traffic than they used to? That’s cos, some time recently, Valve changed the featured front-page games in ‘ Discounts & Events ’ (the non-Daily Deal ones) to be more personalized to logged-in player interests. (A good move to help the little guys, done quietly.)
Here’s a fun site, PS Store DB , which is scraping all PlayStation Store game ratings and creating a ‘Highest Rated weighted by review count’ score. For games with >10k reviews, the top games are Dispatch (4.93/5), Persona 5 Royal (4.91/5), the OG Final Fantasy VII (4.9/5) and Persona 4 Golden (4.9/5), among others…
We don’t talk about AI much, but Nvidia’s DLSS 5 ‘lighting diffusion model’, now shipping in NBA 2K27, is prob. the highest-profile incursion into games so far. There’s a ResetEra thread summarizing a longform Digital Foundry video we found v.helpful: “DLSS 5 best suited for games that are trying to look realistic.”
As passed along by RoadToVR : “Valve has pushed an update to the Steam Link PC VR streaming app on Quest that finally includes the ability to play games via wired connection.” Why now? One commenter notes: “Meta only recently added support for video over USB , and Steam Link could not have implemented wired support without it.”
Errata: on Friday’s August charts we noted that puzzle co-op hit Big Walk had 3m+ PlayStation players (and more downloaders) due to it launching as a PlayStation Plus ‘monthly game’ . But looks like 99%+ of those (not 90%, as we put in the charts) are from PS+ players. (We’ll keep tweaking our PS+ download splits.)
Microlinks: Xbox tells existing Game Pass members its new cloud gaming cap doesn’t apply to them , but only in certain countries; Apple may be working on first-party game controllers ; if you dropped Xbox Game Pass, MS may try to tempt you back with a personal discount price (as low as $16/month for Ultimate.)

Does your Steam demo CCU ‘predict’ outcomes?
How did these titles ‘convert’ their demo CCU? Let’s find out…
Headline: in this era when more Steam games are using pre-release demos to gauge interest & get feedback, we realized: we didn’t formally study the relationship between demo CCU and game CCU . But we can, thx to GameDiscoverCo Pro data (we have concurrents hourly from 2024 & just acquired daily peak CCU back to 2018.)
Firstly, some context: we checked the top 100 top-grossing games of 2026 so far on Steam , and found that 58 of them had a pre-release demo . That includes only 6 of the Top 20 (inc. Windrose, Pragmata) but three quarters (15) of those ranked #81-#100. So when you get below Forza & 007-sized games, it’s extremely common.
Let’s go for a high-level visualization to start. If your game’s demo got more than 50 concurrents on Steam, what was the peak-all time CCU of your game? Well, the median was 3.01x , and here’s the various ranges:
This, we think, is genuinely useful new info, calculated from the 2,569 Steam games we found that launched between Jan. 2024 and Aug. 2026 with a >50 CCU demo . (There were about 55,000 games launched in that time, so that’s only 4.7% of all games.)
So here’s how to think about this 3.01x multiplier - or at least, how we think about it:
Let’s say your game’s demo got 200 CCU on Steam: this means, at median, you might see the full version launch to 600 CCU, which very roughly translates to (if not a pre-orderable game!) about ~12,000 units sold Week 1, and 35,000 units Year 1.
But there’s a lot of moving parts here, both up and down: it’s hardly a fixed ratio! The top 20-30% of demos convert to peak game CCU at 6.24x, and the bottom 20-30% at 1.29x. That’s a 4-5 times difference, pretty quickly. The median isn’t gospel.
Nonetheless, these ratios are important for understanding probability: let’s say your game had a 100 CCU demo, and you need to sell 100k copies in your first year on Steam. To do that, you may need a 16x ‘demo→game’ multiplier.
Is a 16x multiplier (from peak demo CCU to peak game CCU) doable? Absolutely! But you’d need to be in the top 10% of ‘demo to game’ CCU conversion for it to happen. And you need to have a compelling reason why your game would perform that well. (Was the demo underpromoted? Will the main game somehow go more viral?)
Anyhow, we picked out select games with particularly high, near-median, and below-median performance of peak demo to peak game CCU, and here they are:
The high-converters? Mainly games like Megabonk and Escape From Duckov with incredibly strong hook or game design loop that had good interest pre-release (demo CCUs in the hundreds or low thousands), but hit giant CCU highs post-release.
It’s notable there’s not much friendslop in here - partly because friendslop is so inexpensive that it often just launches without a demo? But there’s some co-optional titles that grew over time like Abiotic Factor & LORT, as well as just straight out great ‘sleeper/breakout’ hits like Absolum , Moonlight Peaks , and even Dispatch .
We also wanted to show a range of titles that were closer to ‘normal’ - including solo indie hits like Road To Vostok (3.3x) and AA-ier rhythm action title Dead As Disco (2.34x). If we were using this data to mentally model for your game, we’d probably use 2x-4x as a starting point…
Finally, here’s some games that had stronger demo performance in CCUs than full game performance. (Sorry if you’re featured!) It looks like some of these like Drive Together or Ghostbane are very strong hook for casual demo players, but ‘execution-light’ at commercial release.
Some of the other titles had PR/marketing firepower aimed at the demo rollout, or tried to charge above what the market thinks acceptable for certain styles of game. ($5-$15 is increasingly the norm?) That’s the rough shape of it - please ping us if you see any data discrepancies btw, because we can’t manually check >2,500 games easily.
Finally, we showed this early data to someone who wondered how the median differs, depending on the CCU cut-off. Good question, and the median ‘demo → game’ peak CCU multipliers are like this for demo concurrents: >10 CCU = 2.40x, >50 CCU = 3.01x, >100 CCU = 2.91x, >250 CCU = 2.59x, >500 CCU = 2.41x, >1000 CCU = 2.38x .
(So: as the demo CCUs get bigger, the multiplier and spread gets somewhat smaller, as outliers are removed. Makes total sense to us…)
GameDiscoverCo Show: backing off multiplatform
Finally and ultimately, we’re back with The GameDiscover Show , ft. myself (Simon) and Post Games’ Chris Plante with a bunch of extra insight - sub to the podcast via Apple Music , Spotify & elsewhere (audio), with a video version on YouTube (above).
